name: Cheeses is Born Burger - Comes with baby swiss

recipe.history:
Baby Swiss cheese traces its origins to the rolling green pastures of Switzerland, where Swiss cheese — known locally as Emmental — has been crafted since at least the 13th century in the Emmental valley of the canton of Bern. Traditional Swiss cheese is distinguished by its characteristic holes, called "eyes," formed by carbon dioxide released during fermentation by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria. Baby Swiss is a distinctly American adaptation, developed in the mid-20th century by the Guggisberg Cheese Company in Millersburg, Ohio. Alfred Guggisberg, a Swiss immigrant cheesemaker, created baby Swiss in 1965 by using smaller wheels, a lower-moisture curd, and a shorter aging period — typically four to six weeks versus several months for traditional Emmental. The result is a cheese with smaller, more numerous holes, a creamier, milder flavor, and a supple, ivory-colored paste that melts with extraordinary grace.

Baby Swiss found its way into American burger culture through the mid-century diner boom and the relentless American appetite for melted cheese on everything. While processed American cheese dominated the burger landscape of the 1950s and 60s, the so-called "gourmet burger" movement of the 1970s and 80s pushed chefs and home cooks alike toward more interesting melting cheeses. Baby Swiss, with its gentle nutty sweetness and superior melt, quickly became a favorite alternative to standard Swiss on deli sandwiches and burgers. Its slightly lower sharpness compared to aged Emmental meant it could complement beef without overwhelming it, and its smaller eyes meant it lay flat and melted evenly across a patty, making it aesthetically and practically ideal for the cheeseburger format. By the 1990s, baby Swiss had become a staple of upscale casual burger joints from Ohio to Oregon.

I remember the first time I truly understood baby Swiss. I was twelve years old, standing at the deli counter of a family-owned grocery store in a small Ohio town, watching the counter man hand-slice a thick slab of Guggisberg baby Swiss directly from the wheel. He let me taste a corner of it, and I was stopped in my tracks — it was nothing like the rubbery, factory-wrapped Swiss I'd grown up tolerating on cold-cut sandwiches. This was creamy, yielding, faintly sweet, with just a whisper of nuttiness that lingered on the palate. Years later, when I started making burgers seriously, baby Swiss was the first cheese I reached for when I wanted something that felt both honest and a little elevated. There is something deeply satisfying about watching it drape itself over a sizzling patty, softening into slow, silky folds, becoming something almost inseparable from the beef beneath it.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is not a preference — it is a philosophy, and for beef of quality, it is the only morally defensible choice. At an internal temperature of 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C), the muscle fibers of the patty have contracted just enough to hold their shape while the intramuscular fat has begun to render, basting the meat from within. The result is a center that is warm, deeply pink, and luxuriantly juicy — a texture that no higher temperature can replicate or recover. Beyond medium rare, moisture departs irreversibly, fat finishes rendering into grease rather than juice, and the burger becomes something lesser: drier, tighter, more apologetic. Medium rare is the temperature at which the cow's contribution is honored most fully, and it is the temperature at which baby Swiss finds its truest purpose, melting gently across a patty that still has everything to give.
ingredients: 1 lb (450g) ground beef chuck, 80/20 fat ratio
instructions: 1. Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off.

2. Divide the beef into two equal portions (approximately 8 oz / 227g each). Gently form each into a patty about 3/4 inch thick, taking care not to overwork the meat. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent bulging during cooking.
3. Season both sides of each patty generously with kosher salt, black pepper, and garlic powder immediately before cooking.
4. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat.
5. Place the patties in the skillet. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to develop a deep sear on the first side.
6. Flip the patties once. Cook for 2 minutes on the second side.
7. Lay two slices of baby Swiss cheese over each patty. Cover the skillet with a lid or dome for 1 minute to melt the cheese.

8. Check the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer. The target is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove from heat when this temperature is reached and tent loosely with foil. Rest for 3 minutes — carryover cooking will bring the final temp to approximately 133–137°F.
9. While the patties rest, spread softened butter on the cut sides of the brioche buns. Toast them cut-side down in the residual heat of the skillet for 60–90 seconds until golden.
10. Mix the mayonnaise and Dijon mustard together and spread on both cut sides of each toasted bun.
11. Layer the bottom bun with lettuce, then the rested cheeseburger patty, followed by tomato, red onion, and pickles.
12. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
